title: Venus et Adonis. Atalanta
titleEn: Venus and Adonis; Atalanta's Race — Metamorphoses X.519–635
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 8719b7d375018d4f. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Winged time slips by, and the boy born of his own sister and his own grandfather is a grown man within a few lines — beautiful enough to please Venus. Kissing his mother, the boy with the quiver grazes her breast with an arrow, and the goddess who deals love-wounds does not recognise one: she leaves her own shrines and heaven itself for Adonis, hunts beside him girt like Diana, and warns him to be bold only with animals that run away. Asked why she hates lions, she lies down with him under a poplar and begins the tale of Atalanta — the oracle that told her to flee marriage, the race she set her suitors with death for the loser, and Hippomenes, who sat scorning the suitors and ended by challenging her himself, leaving her arguing with herself over what she now wants to happen.

sentences.t:
Labitur occulte fallitque volatilis aetas,
et nihil est annis velocius.
sentences.l: Winged time glides by in secret and slips past notice, and nothing is swifter than the years.
sentences.i: Time is on the wing; it goes by in secret and is gone before it is seen, and nothing moves faster than the years.
sentences.n: The subject, volatilis aetas, is held to the end, after both its verbs: aetas is a stretch of time, a lifetime or an age, and volatilis makes it winged. fallit is used absolutely, with no object — to cheat, to slip past unnoticed — and occulte, “in secret”, is the adverb of the same idea, said twice for weight. The comparative velocius takes annis as an ablative of comparison, “than the years”. These two lines are Orpheus's, the singer whose song this whole tale is; no character is speaking yet, and the general truth is his own, set down just before the lines that demonstrate it.

sentences.t:
Ille sorore
natus avoque suo, qui conditus arbore nuper,
nuper erat genitus, modo formosissimus infans,
iam iuvenis, iam vir, iam se formosior ipso est:
sentences.l: He, born of his sister and of his own grandfather, who had lately been hidden away in a tree, had lately been brought to birth; a moment ago the loveliest of infants, now a youth, now a man, now he is more beautiful than he himself was:
sentences.i: He who was born of his own sister and his own grandfather — who had so lately been shut inside a tree, so lately been delivered out of it, an infant of surpassing beauty only a moment since — is now a youth, now a man, now more beautiful than he had been himself:
sentences.n: The relationships are exact and they are the point: his mother was his father's daughter, so she is his half-sister and his father is also his grandfather, and the one line says both. conditus arbore is a bare ablative of place without a preposition, “hidden in a tree”, which verse allows freely; erat genitus is a pluperfect passive, “had been brought to birth”. After that the clause is nothing but time-words — nuper twice over, then modo, then iam three times — and the whole growth from newborn to man is done inside two lines, which is the demonstration of what was just claimed about winged time. se formosior ipso is an ablative of comparison in the reflexive: the person he outdoes is his own earlier self.

sentences.t: iam placet et Veneri matrisque ulciscitur ignes.
sentences.l: now he pleases Venus too, and avenges his mother's fires.
sentences.i: now he pleases Venus herself, and pays back the fires his mother was made to feel.
sentences.n: placet takes the dative Veneri, “is pleasing to Venus”, and the et is “even, also”, attached to Veneri rather than to the verb. ulciscitur is deponent — passive in form, active in meaning — so he is the one doing the avenging. ignes, “fires”, is the standing Latin metaphor for the passion of love, and matris ignes are the passion his mother was made to feel; the revenge is that the goddess who caused it will now feel one herself. This is Orpheus's judgement, spoken before Venus has said a word.

sentences.t:
Namque pharetratus dum dat puer oscula matri,
inscius exstanti destrinxit harundine pectus.
sentences.l: For while the quiver-carrying boy was giving his mother kisses, without knowing it he grazed her breast with a shaft standing out of the case.
sentences.i: For as the boy with the quiver was kissing his mother, he grazed her breast, never knowing it, with an arrow that stood out of the quiver.
sentences.n: The quivered boy is Venus's son, named here by his gear rather than by his name. dum with the present indicative dat inside a perfect narrative is the ordinary “while”, and the present tense keeps the kiss going on while the wound happens. exstanti harundine is an ablative of means: harundo is a reed and so an arrow-shaft, and exstanti says it was sticking up out of the quiver, so the wound is an accident of an embrace. inscius, “not knowing”, is nominative and belongs to the boy. destrinxit is “grazed, scraped along” — a scratch, not a shot: the poem is careful that nothing was aimed.

sentences.t:
Laesa manu natum dea reppulit. Altius actum
vulnus erat specie primoque fefellerat ipsam.
sentences.l: Hurt, the goddess pushed her son away with her hand. The wound had been driven deeper than its look, and at first had deceived even her.
sentences.i: Stung, the goddess pushed the boy off with her hand. The wound had gone deeper than it looked, and at first even she was taken in by it.
sentences.n: Laesa is a perfect passive participle agreeing with dea, “having been hurt”, where English wants a clause of its own. actum erat is a pluperfect passive of ago, the verb for driving a weapon home, and specie is an ablative of comparison after altius, “deeper than its appearance”. fefellerat is the same verb of slipping past notice that was used of time at 519, and here it has the goddess for its object, with ipsam, “even her”, pressing the point: the one who deals love-wounds did not recognise one.

sentences.t:
Capta viri forma non iam Cythereia curat
litora, non alto repetit Paphon aequore cinctam
piscosamque Gnidon gravidamve Amathunta metallis;
abstinet et caelo: caelo praefertur Adonis.
sentences.l: Caught by the man's beauty, she no longer cares for the shores of Cythera, does not go back to Paphos ringed by the deep sea, or to fish-thronged Gnidos, or to Amathus heavy with ore; she keeps away from heaven as well: to heaven Adonis is preferred.
sentences.i: Taken by the man's beauty, she no longer cares for the shores of Cythera; she does not go back to Paphos ringed with deep water, or to Gnidos full of fish, or to Amathus weighed down with metal; she stays away from heaven too — Adonis is preferred to heaven.
sentences.n: Cythereia is an adjective here, not a name of the goddess: it agrees with litora, “the Cytherean shores”. The four places are all seats of her own worship, so the list is of the holy places she is neglecting, and it climbs to caelo, heaven itself, repeated across the colon so that the second half of the line answers the first. praefertur is passive with a dative of the thing surpassed — Adonis is put before heaven. gravidam metallis is an ablative with the adjective, “heavy with ores”; Amathus was a mining town. The edition prints Gnidon, where some editions print Cnidon: the same place, spelt with the Greek letter or the Latin one.

sentences.t:
Hunc tenet, huic comes est; adsuetaque semper in umbra
indulgere sibi formamque augere colendo
per iuga, per silvas dumosaque saxa vagatur
fine genu vestem ritu succincta Dianae
hortaturque canes;
sentences.l: Him she holds, to him she is a companion; and she who was always accustomed to indulge herself in the shade and to increase her beauty by tending it now roams over ridges, through woods and bramble-covered rocks, girt as to her dress with the knee for its limit, in Diana's fashion, and cheers on the hounds;
sentences.i: She keeps him beside her, she goes wherever he goes; and the goddess who was always used to taking her ease in the shade and improving her beauty by attending to it now ranges over ridges, through woods and rocks full of briars, her dress caught up knee-high after Diana's manner, calling the hounds on;
sentences.n: adsueta, “accustomed”, takes two plain present infinitives, indulgere and augere, which is the ordinary Latin construction. colendo is an ablative gerund, “by tending”: the verb is the one used of cultivating a field and of paying court to a god, so the beauty she keeps up is something she has been serving. succincta is a perfect participle with vestem as an accusative of respect — “girt as to her dress” — a construction Latin verse borrows from Greek and uses constantly; fine genu is “with the knee as the boundary”. ritu Dianae is an ablative of manner, “in Diana's way”, and the joke is in the name: Venus has dressed as the huntress who wants nothing to do with her.

sentences.t:
tutaeque animalia praedae,
aut pronos lepores aut celsum in cornua cervum,
aut agitat dammas:
sentences.l: and animals that are safe prey — either hares stooping low, or a stag lifted high into his antlers, or fallow deer — she drives:
sentences.i: and she hunts what is safe to hunt: hares running low to the ground, a stag reared up into his antlers, fallow deer.
sentences.n: tutae praedae is a genitive of description hanging on animalia, “animals of safe prey” — game that will not turn on you. The one verb, agitat, arrives only in 539 and governs all three objects, so the list is held open for a line and a half before the reader is told what is being done with it. pronos is “tipped forward”, the shape of a running hare; celsum in cornua puts an accusative of direction with the adjective, “lofty into his antlers”, the height measured by where the antlers reach. The threefold aut … aut … aut counts the list off, and everything on it is chosen for what it is not: the animals she avoids come next.

sentences.t:
a fortibus abstinet apris
raptoresque lupos armatosque unguibus ursos
vitat et armenti saturatos caede leones.
sentences.l: she keeps clear of strong boars, and avoids plundering wolves and bears armed with claws and lions gorged with the slaughter of the herd.
sentences.i: She keeps well away from the strong boars, and gives a wide berth to wolves that carry off their kill, to bears armed with claws, to lions glutted with the slaughter of cattle.
sentences.n: abstinet takes a with the ablative, “holds off from”, while vitat takes a plain accusative, and its three objects straddle the verb: lupos and ursos fill 540 ahead of it, and leones follows it at the end of 541. raptores is a noun used as an adjective, “plunderers, carriers-off”. armatos unguibus is a participle with an ablative of means, “armed with their claws” — the bears are given the vocabulary of soldiers. saturatos caede armenti is “sated with the slaughter of the herd”, caede an ablative with the participle and armenti a genitive of what was slaughtered. The boar heads the list, and it is the boar Venus comes back to in her own words at 550.

sentences.t:
Te quoque, ut hos timeas, siquid prodesse monendo
possit, Adoni, monet,
sentences.l: You too, Adonis, she warns, that you may fear these, if warning could be of any use;
sentences.i: You too, Adonis, she warns — to be afraid of them, if warning can do any good at all.
sentences.n: This is apostrophe: Orpheus turns from telling the story to speaking to Adonis directly, and te and the vocative Adoni are addressed to a man the song has already placed in the past. ut hos timeas is a purpose clause after monet, “she warns so that you may fear them”. siquid prodesse monendo possit is a conditional in the subjunctive, “if warning could be of any use” — the doubt is the singer's, not the goddess's, and it tells the reader in advance how the warning will go. monendo is an ablative gerund, “by warning”. The edition prints siquid as one word.

sentences.t:
“fortis” que “fugacibus esto”
inquit “in audaces non est audacia tuta.
sentences.l: “Be brave toward the ones that run,” she says, “against the bold, boldness is not safe.
sentences.i: “Be bold with the ones that run away,” she says. “Against the ones that dare, daring is not safe.
sentences.n: The line is broken open by its own speech-tags: the connective que is hung on the first word of the quotation and inquit is dropped inside it, so the Latin runs “be-brave”-and “against the fleeing” she-says. esto is the future imperative, the form Latin keeps for standing rules and laws rather than a single order. fugacibus and audaces are adjectives used as nouns, “the ones that run” and “the ones that dare”; fugacibus is a dative with fortis, “brave toward them”, while in with the accusative is “against”. The point turns on audaces and audacia sharing a root: the idiomatic keeps the play with dare and daring, the literal keeps the abstraction with boldness. These are the first words Venus speaks in the part.

sentences.t:
Parce meo, iuvenis, temerarius esse periclo,
neve feras, quibus arma dedit natura, lacesse,
stet mihi ne magno tua gloria.
sentences.l: Spare to be reckless at my cost, young man, and do not provoke wild beasts to which nature has given weapons, lest your glory stand me at a great price.
sentences.i: Do not be rash at my expense, my boy, and do not stir up animals that nature has armed, or your glory will cost me dear.
sentences.n: parce with an infinitive is “forbear to”, a gentler prohibition than a bare imperative, and meo periclo is an ablative, “at my risk”, which puts the danger on her rather than on him. neve … lacesse continues the prohibition with a second imperative. In the relative clause, arma means natural weapons — tusks, claws — which is exactly what separates these animals from the ones she hunts at 537-539. stet … magno is the idiom of price: sto with an ablative of price means “cost”, so what she fears is what she will have to pay. The word order ties the knot, with ne standing third in its own clause between mihi and magno.

sentences.t:
Non movet aetas
nec facies nec quae Venerem movere, leones
saetigerosque sues oculosque animosque ferarum.
sentences.l: Your youth does not move, nor your face, nor the things that have moved Venus — lions, and bristled boars, and the eyes and hearts of wild animals.
sentences.i: Neither your youth nor your looks nor the things that moved Venus move lions, or bristling boars, or the eyes and tempers of beasts.
sentences.n: The three subjects come first — aetas, facies, and the relative clause quae Venerem movere — and the four accusative objects only arrive afterwards, spread over a line and a half, so the sentence says what will not work before it says on whom. movere is the poetic third-person plural perfect, -ere for -erunt, a form this poem uses constantly. Venus names herself in the third person: what won her will not win an animal. oculos animosque ferarum is a pair, the beast's eye and the beast's temper, and the second is the one she means.

sentences.t:
Fulmen habent acres in aduncis dentibus apri,
impetus est fulvis et vasta leonibus ira,
invisumque mihi genus est.”
sentences.l: Fierce boars have a lightning-bolt in their hooked tusks, tawny lions have their charge and a huge anger, and the breed is hated by me.”
sentences.i: The boar carries lightning in his curved tusks, the tawny lion has his charge and his measureless rage — and the whole kind is hateful to me.”
sentences.n: fulmen, the thunderbolt, for a boar's tusk is a stock figure of the hunt, and it is the hardest word in her speech. in aduncis dentibus is “in the hooked teeth”, dens covering the tusk. fulvis leonibus is a dative of the possessor with est: Latin says “there is a charge to the tawny lions” where English says they have one. genus is “the kind, the breed”, and mihi is a dative with the passive adjective invisum, “hated by me”. It is that last clause, not the warning, that Adonis takes up — and it is where Venus stops advising and begins a story.

sentences.t:
Quae causa, roganti
“dicam,” ait “et veteris monstrum mirabere culpae.
sentences.l: To him, asking what the cause was, she says: “I will tell it, and you will wonder at the portent of an old fault.
sentences.i: When he asks what the reason is, “I will tell you,” she says, “and you will wonder at the portent an old offence produced.
sentences.n: Quae causa is an indirect question with its verb left out, “what the cause was”, and it hangs on roganti, a present participle in the dative, “to him asking”: Adonis's question is reported in two words and he never speaks in his own voice. mirabere is the alternative second-person singular future, -bere for -beris, common in verse. monstrum is not simply a monster: it is a thing shown, a portent, and here the portent that a culpa, a fault or a guilt, produced. Everything from 560 to the end of the part is Venus speaking to Adonis in answer to this — a tale inside Orpheus's song, not Orpheus's own narration.

sentences.l: But unaccustomed work has tired me by now, and look — a poplar standing just where it is wanted coaxes us with its shade, and the turf gives a couch;
sentences.i: But I am not used to this work and it has tired me already; and look — there is a poplar exactly where we want it, tempting us with its shade, and the grass makes a bed.
sentences.n: labor insolitus is the hunting she has just been described doing, and insolitus is “unaccustomed” of the person, not of the work. blanditur is deponent, active in sense: the verb of coaxing and flattering that Latin uses of a lover, given here to a tree, with sua umbra an ablative of means. opportuna stands first in its line and does the work of an adverb — the tree is conveniently placed. torus is a couch and a marriage-bed both, and caespes is cut turf; the two nouns together are why the sentence is not only about resting.

sentences.t:
libet hac requiescere tecum”
(et requievit) “humo” pressitque et gramen et ipsum,
inque sinu iuvenis posita cervice reclinis
sic ait ac mediis interserit oscula verbis:
sentences.l: It is a pleasure to rest with you here on this” — and she rested — “ground”; and she pressed down both the grass and the man himself, and lying back with her neck laid in the young man's lap she speaks like this, and sets kisses in among her words:
sentences.i: I should be glad to lie down here with you on this” — and she lay down — “ground”: and she pressed both grass and boy, and lay back with her head in the young man's lap, and speaks, slipping kisses in between the words:
sentences.n: The joke is in the word order and nowhere else. Her phrase is hac … humo, “on this ground”, and Orpheus cuts it in half to report, in a bracket, that she was lying down before she had reached the noun. libet is impersonal with an infinitive, “it is a pleasure to”. pressit takes two objects joined by et … et, gramen and ipsum, the grass and the man, with one verb serving both. posita cervice is an ablative absolute, “her neck having been laid”, and in sinu iuvenis says where. interserit is “sets in between”, with mediis verbis an ablative, “in the middle of her words”: the whole tale that follows is told in that posture, which is worth keeping in mind while reading it.

sentences.l: “Perhaps you have heard that some woman beat swift men in a contest of running. That report was no fable: for she was beating them;
sentences.i: “You may have heard of a woman who beat fast men in a footrace. That report was no invention: she did beat them, over and over;
sentences.n: forsitan takes the subjunctive, audieris, “perhaps you have heard”; superasse is the syncopated perfect infinitive of supero, for superavisse, in indirect statement after it, with aliquam as its accusative subject. The woman is not named for five more lines: Venus starts from a rumour her listener may already have met and only gives it a name at 565. rumor ille is set against fabula, an invented story — the distinction is between a true report and a tale. superabat is imperfect against the perfect infinitive before it, and the change of tense is the change from a single fact to a habit: she went on beating them.

sentences.t:
nec dicere posses,
laude pedum formaene bono praestantior esset.
sentences.l: nor could you have said whether she was more outstanding in the credit of her feet or in the gift of her beauty.
sentences.i: nor could you have said which she was better in, the credit her running earned her or the endowment of her beauty.
sentences.n: posses is a potential subjunctive in past time, “you could not have said”, and the “you” is Adonis, lying beside her. What follows is an indirect question with the first limb unmarked and -ne hung on the second, laude … formaene bono: Latin can leave the first alternative bare where English has to supply “whether”. praestantior takes both ablatives as ablatives of respect. laus pedum is the credit her feet earned her; formae bonum is a genitive of definition, the good thing that is her beauty.

sentences.t:
Scitanti deus huic de coniuge “coniuge” dixit
“nil opus est, Atalanta, tibi: fuge coniugis usum!
sentences.l: To her, as she enquired about a husband, the god said: “Of a husband you have no need, Atalanta: run from the use of a husband!
sentences.i: When she asked the god about a husband, “A husband,” he said, “is the one thing you have no need of, Atalanta — run from ever having one!
sentences.n: The answer begins with the very word the question ended on: de coniuge closes her asking and coniuge opens his reply, in the same case, so the oracle throws her own word back at her. opus est takes an ablative of the thing needed and a dative of the person needing it, coniuge … tibi, “there is no need to you of a husband”. scitanti is a present participle in the dative agreeing with huic, “to her as she enquired”. usus is the plain word for the use or enjoyment of a thing, and Latin will use it of a marriage as of a possession. This is a third voice: Venus quoting a god, inside her own tale, inside Orpheus's song.

sentences.t: nec tamen effugies teque ipsa viva carebis.”
sentences.l: and yet you will not escape, and, alive, you will go without your own self.”
sentences.i: and yet you will not escape it: you will lose your own self while you are still living.”
sentences.n: The oracle turns the same verb against itself — fuge in the line before, its compound effugies here — so the order and the prediction contradict each other on purpose. careo takes an ablative of what one goes without, te ipsa; viva is nominative, agreeing with the subject and not with te ipsa, so it is she who is alive while she is without herself. What the words mean is left dark, as an oracle's words are; nothing in the part explains them, and Venus reports them without comment.

sentences.t:
Territa sorte dei per opacas innuba silvas
vivit et instantem turbam violenta procorum
condicione fugat,
sentences.l: Terrified by the god's oracle, unmarried she lives among shadowy woods, and, violent, puts to flight the pressing crowd of her suitors by a condition,
sentences.i: Frightened by the god's answer, she lives unmarried in the shade of the woods, and violently drives off the crowd of suitors pressing round her with a condition —
sentences.n: sors is the lot drawn at an oracle, and so the oracle's answer itself. innuba, “unwedded”, is a poetic adjective agreeing with the subject and standing where a verb would help: it is the whole of her obedience to the god. instantem is a present participle with turbam, “pressing, standing over her”. violenta is nominative and belongs to the subject, not to condicione: the violence is hers, and the term she sets is left with no adjective at all. The line-end still separates the two words — violenta stands late in 568, which closes on procorum, and condicione opens 569. The condition itself comes at once, in her own words.

sentences.t:
nec “sum potienda, nisi” inquit
“victa prius cursu.
sentences.l: and she says: “I am not to be got, unless beaten first in a race.
sentences.i: and “You cannot have me,” she says, “unless you have beaten me in a race first.
sentences.n: potienda is a gerundive with sum — the passive periphrastic, “I am to be got, I must be won”. The verb is potior, which normally takes an ablative and means to get possession of a thing; used passively of herself, it makes her the property in the transaction. victa is a perfect participle agreeing with the unexpressed “I”, so the ellipsis is complete: nisi ego victa sim. The speech-tag inquit is dropped inside the quotation, between nisi and what nisi governs, which is why the Latin looks broken and is not.

sentences.t:
Pedibus contendite mecum:
praemia veloci coniunx thalamique dabuntur,
mors pretium tardis. Ea lex certaminis esto.”
sentences.l: Race me on foot: to the swift man a wife and a marriage-chamber will be given as prizes, death the payment for the slow. Let that be the law of the contest.”
sentences.i: Race me on foot. For the fast man the prize will be a bride and a marriage bed; for the slow, death is the payment. Let that be the rule of the contest.”
sentences.n: contendite is plural: she is answering the whole crowd of 568, not one man. praemia stands in apposition to coniunx thalamique, “a wife and a marriage-chamber, as prizes”, and veloci is a dative of the person who gets them. The second half drops the verb altogether — mors pretium tardis, three words, no est — and pretium, a price paid, is set against praemia, a prize won, so both halves sound like one transaction. esto is the future imperative again, the form of laws, matching lex.

sentences.t:
Illa quidem inmitis: sed (tanta potentia formae est)
venit ad hanc legem temeraria turba procorum.
sentences.l: She, admittedly, was without pity — but such is the power of beauty — a reckless crowd of suitors came to those terms.
sentences.i: Merciless, no question about it — but beauty has that much power: a reckless crowd of suitors came in on those terms.
sentences.n: Illa quidem inmitis has no verb at all, and quidem concedes the point before sed takes it back: the shape of the sentence is a shrug. The parenthesis is Venus's own aside, spoken to the man lying beside her, not Orpheus's. inmitis is the edition's spelling of immitis, the older unassimilated form, kept here as everywhere and not an error. legem picks up lex from 572, so ad hanc legem is “to the terms she had just laid down”. temeraria is the word Venus herself used of Adonis at 545, temerarius: recklessness at somebody else's cost is what joins her warning to her tale.

sentences.t:
Sederat Hippomenes cursus spectator iniqui
et “petitur cuiquam per tanta pericula coniunx?”
dixerat ac nimios iuvenum damnarat amores.
sentences.l: Hippomenes had sat as a watcher of that unfair race, and had said, “Is a wife sought by anybody through dangers as great as these?” and had condemned the excessive loves of the young men.
sentences.i: Hippomenes had been sitting there watching that one-sided race, and had said, “Would anyone go after a wife through danger like this?” — and had condemned those young men for loving beyond all measure.
sentences.n: Three pluperfects in a row — sederat, dixerat, damnarat — put the whole of his contempt down before the moment the story is actually about: it had all happened before he looked at her. damnarat is syncopated for damnaverat. spectator stands in apposition to Hippomenes, “as a spectator”, and iniqui with cursus is “unfair” in the plain sense that the terms are not equal. cuiquam is a dative of the agent with the passive petitur, “is sought by anyone”, a construction chiefly of verse. nimios amores is “loves beyond measure”, and nimius is a word of judgement — his.

sentences.t:
Ut faciem et posito corpus velamine vidit,
quale meum, vel quale tuum, si femina fias,
obstipuit tollensque manus “ignoscite,” dixit
“quos modo culpavi.
sentences.l: When he saw her face and her body with the covering laid aside — a body such as mine, or such as yours would be, if you were to turn woman — he was struck dumb, and lifting his hands he said: “Forgive me, you whom I blamed a moment ago.
sentences.i: When he saw her face, and her body with the covering off — a body like mine, or like yours would be if you turned woman — he stood dumbstruck, and raised his hands and said: “Forgive me, you that I blamed just now.
sentences.n: posito velamine is an ablative absolute, “the covering having been laid aside”, which English turns into “with it off”: the runners stripped. The middle line is Venus speaking in her own person, in the middle of her tale — quale meum is her own body, and si femina fias is a present subjunctive of an imagined case, “if you were to turn woman”. She is telling the man in her lap that the girl's body was like hers, and like his. ignoscite is plural, and ignosco governs a dative; the dative itself is left unexpressed, and the men addressed are named only by the relative clause quos modo culpavi, whose antecedent is swallowed entirely: “you whom I blamed just now”. The men he is apologising to are the dead ones.

sentences.t:
Nondum mihi praemia nota,
quae peteretis, erant.”
sentences.l: The prizes were not yet known to me, the prizes you were competing for.”
sentences.i: I did not yet know what the prize was that you were going after.”
sentences.n: nota erant with the dative mihi is “were known to me”, the ordinary Latin way of saying one knew a thing. praemia is her own word from 571, so he concedes her terms in her vocabulary. peteretis is imperfect subjunctive, second person plural, addressed to the dead suitors, and the subjunctive in the relative clause makes it say what kind of prize rather than merely which — “the sort of thing you were after”. The apology takes a line and a half, and the next word in the poem is Laudando.

sentences.t:
Laudando concipit ignes
et, ne quis iuvenum currat velocius, optat
invidiaque timet.
sentences.l: In praising her he catches fire, and wishes that none of the young men may run faster, and out of jealousy is afraid.
sentences.i: Praising her, he takes fire himself, and hopes none of the young men can run faster, and is afraid out of jealousy.
sentences.n: Laudando is an ablative gerund, “by praising”: admiring her out loud is what lights him. concipit ignes is the same metaphor of fire for love used of the mother's ignes at 524. ne quis … currat is a substantive clause of purpose after optat, “he wishes that nobody may run”, and quis after ne is the indefinite “anyone”. invidia is an ablative of cause, “out of jealousy”. Three verbs in a line and a half are the whole of his fall, and the man doing the falling is the one who had just called these loves excessive.

sentences.t:
“Sed cur certaminis huius
intemptata mihi fortuna relinquitur?” inquit
“audentes deus ipse iuvat.”
sentences.l: “But why is the chance of this contest left untried by me?” he says. “The god himself helps those who dare.”
sentences.i: “But why should I leave the luck of this contest untried?” he says. “Heaven itself helps the daring.”
sentences.n: mihi is a dative of the agent with the passive relinquitur, “is left by me”, which the idiomatic layer turns round into an active. intemptata is the edition's unassimilated spelling and is not an error. fortuna here is the chance the contest offers, not the goddess. audentes is a present participle used as a noun, “those who are daring”, and deus ipse is bare — “the god himself”, any god, heaven. The sentence is a proverb, and he says it to himself to talk himself into a race whose loser is put to death.

sentences.t:
Dum talia secum
exigit Hippomenes, passu volat alite virgo.
sentences.l: While Hippomenes is turning such things over with himself, the girl flies by with winged step.
sentences.i: While Hippomenes is still arguing it out with himself, the girl comes flying past on wings at her feet.
sentences.n: exigit with secum is “drives through with oneself”, the Latin for turning a thing over in one's mind; the same verb is used of weighing goods out. dum with the present indicative inside a past narrative is the standing “while”, and it does the work of the whole sentence: the race has begun while he was still deliberating. passu alite is an ablative of manner, “with winged step”, ales being the adjective for winged. virgo, the plain word for an unmarried girl, is the noun the tale keeps for her here and again at 601.

sentences.t:
Quae quamquam Scythica non setius ire sagitta
Aonio visa est iuveni, tamen ille decorem
miratur magis; et cursus facit ipse decorem.
sentences.l: And although she seemed to the Aonian youth to go no more slowly than a Scythian arrow, still he wonders more at her beauty; and the running itself makes the beauty.
sentences.i: And though she seemed to the young Boeotian to travel no slower than a Scythian arrow, it was her grace he wondered at more — and the running is what made the grace.
sentences.n: Quae is a connecting relative opening the sentence — “and she”, not “who” — which English turns into an ordinary pronoun. non setius is “not less”, with Scythica sagitta an ablative of comparison, “than a Scythian arrow”: the Scythians were the archers of the Greek imagination. Aonio iuveni is a dative with visa est, “seemed to”; Aonia is Boeotia, so the adjective says where Hippomenes came from, which he confirms himself at 605. decorem closes both 589 and 590, and the second sentence turns the first inside out: what he admires is not something the speed interrupts but something the speed produces.

sentences.l: The breeze carries back the ankle-ribbons snatched from her swift soles, and her hair is thrown across her ivory back, and so are the knee-bands that lay below the hollows of her knees with their embroidered hem;
sentences.i: The wind takes the ribbons streaming from her fast feet and blows them back, and her hair is flung across her ivory back, and so are the knee-bands under the hollows of her knees with their embroidered edge;
sentences.n: Everything in motion here is dress, and the sentence is built to be looked at rather than followed. ablata is a perfect participle with talaria, “carried off”, and citis plantis is an ablative of separation, “from her swift soles”; talaria are the ankle-pieces, the word used of the winged sandals of a god. iactantur is passive with crines for its subject, and in terga per eburnea the preposition stands between the noun and its adjective, which verse allows freely. quae … genualia is a relative with its antecedent drawn inside the clause, and it is a second subject of iactantur, split across the line-end — quaeque closes 592 and genualia stands in 593. picto limbo is an ablative of description, “with an embroidered border”.

sentences.t:
inque puellari corpus candore ruborem
traxerat, haud aliter, quam cum super atria velum
candida purpureum simulatas inficit umbras.
sentences.l: and her body had drawn a redness across its girlish whiteness, not otherwise than when a purple awning over a courtyard stains what is white and makes counterfeit shadows.
sentences.i: and a blush had spread over the white of her girl's body — no differently from the way a purple awning above a courtyard stains what is white beneath it and lays down a shade that is not one.
sentences.n: traxerat is pluperfect, “had drawn”: the blush is already there before the simile arrives to explain it. in … candore is in with the ablative, “over the whiteness”, the preposition separated from its noun by both puellari and corpus. The comparison is domestic and Roman: a velum is the coloured cloth stretched over an open courtyard against the sun, and the light through it falls on the white below as colour. candida is a neuter plural accusative, “the white things”, the object of inficit, and simulatas umbras is a second accusative in apposition to it, “counterfeit shadows” — the awning does not shade, it dyes, which is exactly why the comparison suits a blush. haud aliter quam cum is the standard formula for such similes, “no otherwise than when”.

sentences.t:
Dum notat haec hospes, decursa novissima meta est
et tegitur festa victrix Atalanta corona.
sentences.l: While the stranger is noticing all this, the last turning-post has been run past, and Atalanta the winner is covered with a festival garland.
sentences.i: While the visitor is taking all this in, the last post is passed, and Atalanta wins and is covered with a festival wreath.
sentences.n: hospes is “the stranger, the guest”: Hippomenes is an outsider in this crowd, and the noun keeps him one — Atalanta calls him by it again at 620. decursa est is perfect passive of decurro, “has been run down, run past”; meta is the turning-post of a racecourse, and novissima is “last” in the ordinary Latin sense of “newest, most recent”. tegitur is passive, “is covered”, with festa corona an ablative of means. The whole race, from start to garland, takes the time the man spends looking at her clothes.

sentences.t: Dant gemitum victi penduntque ex foedere poenas.
sentences.l: The beaten give a groan and pay the penalties under the agreement.
sentences.i: The losers groan and pay the penalty the bargain laid down.
sentences.n: poenas pendere is the standing idiom for paying a penalty, and here it is not a figure at all: the penalty is the death fixed at 572. ex foedere is “in accordance with the compact”, and foedus is the word for a formal treaty between states, so the killing is put into the vocabulary of law rather than of murder — which is how Venus chooses to tell it. victi is a perfect participle used as a noun, “the beaten men”. What happens to them is one line long.

sentences.t:
Non tamen eventu iuvenis deterritus horum
constitit in medio, vultuque in virgine fixo
“quid facilem titulum superando quaeris inertes?
mecum confer!” ait.
sentences.l: Not put off, though, by the outcome of these men, the young man took his stand in the middle, and with his face fixed on the girl: “Why do you look for an easy distinction by beating slow men? Match yourself with me!” he says.
sentences.i: The young man, undeterred by what became of them, took his stand in the middle of the ground, fixed his eyes on the girl, and said: “Why go after a cheap title by beating men with no speed in them? Try me!”
sentences.n: eventu horum is an ablative of cause with deterritus, “by the outcome of these”, horum being the dead men of the line before. constitit in medio is the language of stepping out into an arena. vultu in virgine fixo is an ablative absolute, “his face having been fixed on the girl”, which English wants as a clause of its own. superando is an ablative gerund with inertes for its object, “by beating the slow” — a Latin gerund can govern an accusative where an English one cannot. titulus is the inscription that records an honour, so an easy titulus is credit cheaply got. confer is the imperative of confero, “bring together, match”, and mecum confer is the challenge in two words.

sentences.t:
“Seu me fortuna potentem
fecerit, a tanto non indignabere vinci:
sentences.l: “Whether fortune makes me the one with the power, you will not think it beneath you to be beaten by so great a man:
sentences.i: “If fortune makes me the stronger, you will not think it a disgrace to be beaten by a man of my standing:
sentences.n: seu is the first limb of a pair; its answering seu comes at 607, so the whole argument is that she gains either way. fecerit is future perfect, “shall have made”, where English is content with a present. potentem is a predicate accusative with it, “made me the one with the power”, that is, the winner. indignabere is deponent — active in sense — and second person singular future, the -bere ending for -beris; it takes the passive infinitive vinci, “to be beaten”, and a with the ablative of the person, a tanto, “by one so great”. What follows is two lines explaining how great.

sentences.l: for my father is Megareus of Onchestus, and to him Neptune is grandfather; I am the great-grandson of the king of the waters, and my worth does not fall short of my birth;
sentences.i: for my father is Megareus of Onchestus, and Neptune is his grandfather; I am the great-grandson of the king of the waters — and what I am is not below what I come from;
sentences.n: mihi and illi are datives of the possessor with est, which Latin prefers to a verb for “have”: “there is to me a father, Megareus”, “there is to him a grandfather, Neptune”. illi is Megareus, so the line runs Neptune, an unnamed child, Megareus, Hippomenes — which is precisely what pronepos, great-grandson, says, and exactly the count Atalanta makes at 617. Onchestius is an adjective of place, from Onchestus, which is in the same country the poem called Aonia at 589. citra with the accusative is “on this side of”, so nec virtus citra genus est is “my worth does not stop short of my descent”.

sentences.t:
seu vincar, habebis
Hippomene victo magnum et memorabile nomen.”
sentences.l: or if I am beaten, you will have, with Hippomenes beaten, a great and memorable name.”
sentences.i: or if I lose, then in the beating of Hippomenes you will have a name worth remembering.”
sentences.n: vincar opens the second limb of the seu … seu pair, “or if I am beaten”: the form would serve equally as a present subjunctive, but the future perfect indicative fecerit in the first limb makes it the future passive. Hippomene victo is an ablative absolute, “Hippomenes having been beaten”, and it carries the whole of the second half of his argument: his defeat would be her credit. He puts his own name into it, in the ablative, which is itself a claim that the name is already worth something. Hippomene is a Greek ablative ending, kept as Greek names are in Latin verse. The speech closes on nomen, the thing men race for.

sentences.t:
Talia dicentem molli Schoeneia vultu
adspicit et dubitat, superari an vincere malit.
sentences.l: The daughter of Schoeneus looks with a soft face at him saying such things, and hesitates whether she would rather be beaten or win.
sentences.i: Schoeneus's daughter looks at him while he speaks, and her face is soft, and she cannot tell whether she would rather lose or win.
sentences.n: Schoeneia is a Greek patronymic adjective used as a noun, “the daughter of Schoeneus”, and it is how the tale names Atalanta here. Talia dicentem is a present participle in the accusative, the object of adspicit — “him saying such things” — and it stands first, before the person doing the looking. molli vultu is an ablative of description belonging to her, not to him: the change is in her face. dubitat introduces a deliberative indirect question with an, superari an vincere malit, “whether she would rather be beaten or win”, and superari is passive, so the two possibilities are the two ends of one race.

sentences.t:
Atque ita “quis deus hunc formosis” inquit “iniquus
perdere vult caraeque iubet discrimine vitae
coniugium petere hoc? Non sum, me iudice, tanti. —
sentences.l: And so: “What god, unfriendly to the beautiful,” she says, “wants to destroy this one, and orders him to seek this marriage at the hazard of his dear life? I am not worth so much, with me for judge. —
sentences.i: And so: “What god has it in for the beautiful,” she says, “that he wants this one destroyed and makes him go after this marriage at the risk of his own dear life? I am not worth that much, to my own mind. —
sentences.n: The question keeps its adjective back to the end of the line, quis deus … iniquus, and formosis is a dative with it, “unfriendly to the beautiful” — a class in which she puts him and herself together. perdere vult and iubet … petere are two constructions with the same subject, the god. discrimine vitae is an ablative, “at the hazard of his life”, discrimen being the point at which a thing is decided and so the risk. me iudice is an ablative absolute of the barest kind, two nouns with no participle, “with me as judge”. The dash at the end of 613 is the edition's, marking where her mind turns: she argues with herself in blocks and the printer has marked the joins.

sentences.t:
Nec forma tangor (poteram tamen hac quoque tangi),
sed quod adhuc puer est: non me movet ipse, sed aetas.
sentences.l: Nor am I touched by his beauty — though I could have been touched by that too — but by the fact that he is still a boy: he himself does not move me, but his age does.
sentences.i: It is not his beauty that touches me — though it could have, that too — but that he is still a boy: it is not him that moves me, it is his age.
sentences.n: tangor is passive, with forma an ablative of the thing that touches, and the parenthesis then admits in the imperfect poteram exactly what the main clause has just denied. quod adhuc puer est is a substantive clause, “the fact that he is still a boy”, hung on sed as though it were another ablative like forma — the Latin runs the two on as one kind of thing, which is part of why the distinction sounds thin. movet is the verb Venus used at 547, non movet aetas, and she used it to say that age moved nothing; here age is the only thing that moves.

sentences.t: Quid quod inest virtus et mens interrita leti?
sentences.l: What of the fact that there is courage in him, and a mind undaunted at death?
sentences.i: And what of the courage in him, and a mind that death cannot frighten?
sentences.n: Quid quod is the standing formula for adding a further point in an argument, “what of the fact that”, and she uses it three times running from here — the shape of a speech for the defence. inest is “is in”, with the person left to be understood from the context. interrita is a negative compound, “unfrightened”, and leti is a genitive of the thing not feared, which Latin allows with adjectives of this kind. letum is the high word for death, not the plain mors she used when she fixed the terms at 572.

sentences.t: Quid quod ab aequorea numeratur origine quartus?
sentences.l: What of the fact that he is reckoned fourth from a sea-born beginning?
sentences.i: What of his being counted fourth in descent from the sea?
sentences.n: numeratur is passive, “is counted”, and quartus is a predicate nominative with it. Counting Neptune first, the line is Neptune, his child, Megareus, Hippomenes — which is the descent he claimed at 605-606, so she has been listening closely enough to do the arithmetic. aequorea origine is an ablative with ab, “from a sea beginning”, and aequoreus is the adjective of aequor, the level open sea, standing in for the god's name.

sentences.t:
Quid quod amat tantique putat conubia nostra,
ut pereat, si me fors illi dura negarit?
sentences.l: What of the fact that he loves, and reckons a marriage with me at such a price that he would perish, if a hard chance should deny me to him?
sentences.i: What of his loving me, and valuing marriage with me so high that he would die if a hard turn of luck denied me to him?
sentences.n: tanti is a genitive of value with putat, “reckons at so much”, and it picks up her own tanti at 613, where she said she was not worth so much: the third Quid quod answers the sentence she started with. conubia nostra is a poetic plural, and nostra is the plural standing for “my”. ut pereat is a result clause after tanti, “so much that he would die”. negarit is syncopated for negaverit. fors is chance, and dura is the adjective she gives it — she is already speaking as though the outcome were not hers to settle, though it is entirely hers.

sentences.t:
Dum licet, hospes, abi thalamosque relinque cruentos:
coniugium crudele meum est. Tibi nubere nulla
nolet, et optari potes a sapiente puella. —
sentences.l: While it is permitted, stranger, go away and leave the bloodstained marriage-chamber: marriage with me is a cruel thing. No girl will be unwilling to marry you, and you can be wished for by a sensible one. —
sentences.i: Go, stranger, while you still can, and leave this bloody marriage behind: marriage with me is a cruel business. There is not a girl who would not have you, and a girl with sense could want you. —
sentences.n: Dum licet is impersonal, “while it is permitted”, and hospes keeps the noun the poem used of him at 597: he is still the stranger to her. thalamos is a poetic plural for the marriage-chamber, and cruentos is literally bloodstained — the bride's room is where the losers' deaths are counted. coniugium crudele meum est leaves the possessive to do the work: marriage, cruel, mine. nulla nolet is a double negative used as a strong positive, “there is no girl who will be unwilling”. optari potes a sapiente puella is passive with an ablative of the agent, “you can be wished for by a girl with sense” — she is describing, in the passive, a woman who is not herself.

sentences.t: Cur tamen est mihi cura tui tot iam ante peremptis?
sentences.l: And yet why is there any care of you in me, when so many have already been done away with before?
sentences.i: And yet why should I care about you at all, with so many killed before you?
sentences.n: est mihi cura is a dative of the possessor again, “there is a concern to me”, and tui is an objective genitive, “of you” — the genitive of the pronoun tu, not the possessive adjective. tot iam ante peremptis is an ablative absolute whose noun is the bare pronoun tot, “so many”, with peremptis for its participle: “so many having already been done away with before”. perimo is a cold verb, to make an end of a thing, and it is her word for what she did to them. tamen turns the whole block back on itself: everything she has just said in his favour is now what she is asking herself to explain.

sentences.t: Viderit!
sentences.l: Let him look to it!
sentences.i: That is his affair!
sentences.n: viderit is a perfect subjunctive of video used as a jussive, and it is the standing Latin idiom for washing one's hands of a thing: let him see to it, his business. One word stands as a whole sentence, and it is the point at which she stops arguing for him.

sentences.t:
Intereat, quoniam tot caede procorum
admonitus non est agiturque in taedia vitae. —
sentences.l: Let him die, since he has not been warned by the killing of so many suitors and is being driven into a loathing of life. —
sentences.i: Let him die, then, since the killing of so many suitors has not warned him off, and he is being driven into a disgust with living. —
sentences.n: Intereat is a jussive subjunctive, “let him die”, matching viderit just before it. quoniam takes the indicative and offers her reason as a fact. tot caede procorum is an ablative of means with admonitus, “warned by the slaughter of so many suitors”, and caede is the same noun used of the lions at 541: the word does not change when the killing is hers. agitur is passive, “is driven”, and in taedia vitae is “into a weariness of life”, taedia a poetic plural. The dash is again the edition's, closing another block of the argument.

sentences.t:
Occidet hic igitur, voluit quia vivere mecum,
indignamque necem pretium patietur amoris?
sentences.l: Shall he die, then, because he wanted to live with me, and shall he suffer an undeserved killing as the price of loving?
sentences.i: So he is to die because he wanted to live with me, and take an undeserved death as the price of love?
sentences.n: The future indicatives Occidet and patietur are used as a question of outrage: the tense treats the thing as already settled, which is what she cannot accept. quia takes the indicative, voluit, and the contrast is exact — what he wanted was vivere, to live, and what he gets is occidet. pretium is her own word from 572, where the price for the slow was death; indignam is a judgement passed on her own rule. patietur is deponent, active in sense, “he will suffer”; nex is a killing, from neco.

sentences.t: Non erit invidiae victoria nostra ferendae.
sentences.l: My victory will not be one of an ill-will to be borne.
sentences.i: The hatred my winning brings will be past bearing.
sentences.n: invidiae ferendae is a genitive of description with erit, “will be of an ill-will that can be borne”, with the gerundive ferendae, “to be borne”, inside the phrase; English has to unpack the whole of it into a clause. invidia is what other people feel about you — envy, ill-will, blame — so the fear named here is not of guilt but of what will be said. nostra is the plural for “my”, as at 618. The sentence has no verb but erit, and it is the argument that settles her: not that he would die, but that she would be blamed for it.

sentences.t:
Sed non culpa mea est. Utinam desistere velles,
aut, quoniam es demens, utinam velocior esses!
sentences.l: But the fault is not mine. If only you were willing to give it up — or, since you are out of your senses, if only you were faster!
sentences.i: But the fault is not mine. I wish you would give it up — or, since you are mad, I wish you were faster!
sentences.n: culpa is the word Venus used at 553 of the old fault her whole story is meant to explain; Atalanta uses it here of herself, in order to deny it. utinam with the imperfect subjunctive, velles and esses, is a wish about what is not the case now, and she makes two of them in one sentence, the second giving up on the first. demens is not a light word — it is the loss of one's mind — and she says it to him. Between them the two wishes are her whole position: she wants him gone, and if he will not go she wants him to win.

sentences.t: A! quam virgineus puerili vultus in ore est!
sentences.l: Ah! how maidenly the look is on that boyish face!
sentences.i: Ah, how girlish the look is on that boy's face!
sentences.n: quam with an adjective is “how”, and the line is an exclamation with no verb but est. virgineus is the adjective of virgo, the noun the tale has been using of Atalanta herself at 587 and 601, so what she sees in his face is her own quality; vultus is the look or expression and os is the face it sits in. The edition prints A as a separate exclamation with its own mark, and prints it again at the head of the next line; some editions read at, “but”, which would make this a turn in the argument rather than a cry.

sentences.t: A! miser Hippomene, nollem tibi visa fuissem!
sentences.l: Ah, unhappy Hippomenes, I could wish I had not been seen by you!
sentences.i: Ah, poor Hippomenes, I wish you had never set eyes on me!
sentences.n: Hippomene is a vocative, and a Greek one — Greek names keep Greek endings in Latin verse. nollem is a potential subjunctive of nolo, “I should not wish”, and it governs visa fuissem, a pluperfect subjunctive passive with the periphrastic fuissem for essem: “that I had been seen by you”. tibi is a dative of the agent with that passive, “by you”. She has turned from arguing with herself to addressing him by name; the second person has been there since Dum licet, hospes, abi at 620.

sentences.t:
Vivere dignus eras. Quod si felicior essem,
nec mihi coniugium fata importuna negarent,
unus eras, cum quo sociare cubilia vellem.”
sentences.l: You were worthy to live. But if I were luckier, and harsh fates were not denying me a marriage, you were the one man with whom I should want to share a bed.”
sentences.i: You deserved to live. If my luck were better, and the fates were not so harsh as to deny me marriage, you would be the one man I would want to share a bed with.”
sentences.n: dignus takes a plain infinitive, vivere, where prose would use a relative clause. Quod si is “but if”, the connecting relative quod hardened into a particle; the edition prints it as two words. essem and negarent are imperfect subjunctives of an unreal present condition, but the main clause is the indicative eras, “you were” — Latin uses the indicative here where English wants “you would be”, and the effect is to state the thing as settled fact rather than as a possibility. sociare cubilia is “to share a bed”, cubile the sleeping-place, and vellem is a further subjunctive inside the relative clause. Her speech ends on the very marriage the oracle at 565 told her to run from.
